 Apache County’s 2024 Election Was Worse Than Reported, Records Show. Now, It Faces Another Test at the Polls.
 A Votebeat and AZCIR investigation found that preventable failures added to the county’s history of disenfranchising Navajo voters.
 News
 Ship Rock, located in New Mexico, looms like a distant castle from the rural highways of northeastern Apache County. Voters in New Mexico have different protections than in Arizona thanks to New Mexico’s Native American Voting Rights Act, which allows Native American communities to have a say in polling locations, ballot box placements, and precinct boundaries. 
 Ash Ponders for Votebeat
 By Sasha Hupka , Sasha Hupka 
 Sasha Hupka is a contributor for The Fulcrum, a nonpartisan publication dedicated to strengthening democracy by fostering informed civic engagement and elevating diverse perspectives. See More Writings by author 
 Adriana Navarro Adriana Navarro 
 Adriana Navarro is a contributor for The Fulcrum, a nonpartisan publication dedicated to strengthening democracy by fostering informed civic engagement and elevating diverse perspectives. See More Writings by author 
 Nov 19, 2026 
 APACHE COUNTY, Ariz. — As Arizona readies itself for a contentious midterm election, voters in remote, windswept Apache County are hoping this time will be different.
 The mammoth county is known for pine-topped mountains and rolling high desert hills. It’s also home to a large swath of the country’s largest Native American reservation — the Navajo Nation, which makes up its northern half.
 Voters there have been let down many times before. In the 2020 and 2022 elections, the Nation filed emergency lawsuits against Apache County to extend polling hours — a result of voting sites opening late, per court records.
 Then, in 2024, the county experienced an election meltdown on an entirely different scale.
 A Navajo Nation building is pictured in Window Rock, Ariz., on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026. A large swath of the reservation, which is the largest in the country, falls into cash-strapped, remote Apache County. (Ash Ponders for Votebeat) It started less than half an hour after polls opened. Rita Vaughan, then the county’s elections director, wrote what would prove to be a consequential email to her team at 6:27 a.m.: “All printers are not working with poll books.”
 Within hours, the voting process had slowed to a crawl — and, in some cases, appeared to halt entirely. There were reports of two- to three-hour lines at some polling places.
 In public statements and, later, in court, the county blamed malfunctioning ballot printers for the fiasco. They maintained that voters could still vote via backup options like emergency, preprinted ballots and accessible voting machines. They said that staff fixed the problems expeditiously and voting never paused across the reservation.
 There’s just one problem with their explanation: It’s not what actually happened.
 The issue that day stemmed from the county’s electronic pollbooks, not its printers — and it caused a complete breakdown, according to an investigation by Votebeat and the Arizona Center for Investigative Reporting. Records show a combination of technical glitches, communication shortfalls, understaffing, and poor preparation disenfranchised voters in Apache County.
 To reconstruct what happened, Votebeat and AZCIR examined thousands of pages of court documents, voting records, and county emails — some of which the county took 16 months to hand over. Reporters also interviewed voters and witnesses and repeatedly attempted to interview multiple county officials, all of whom either didn’t respond to requests for comment or declined to talk on the record.
 The investigation found that the cash-strapped, rural county appeared fundamentally unprepared for the 2024 election — and raises concerns about the county’s readiness for another high-stakes election now just days away.
 Campaign signs crowd a corner in Lukachukai, Ariz., on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026. Voters there are preparing to vote in the first major election since 2024, when widespread technical issues threw voting into chaos in Apache County. (Ash Ponders for Votebeat)
 A previously unreported letter sent to county officials by Arizona Secretary of State Adrian Fontes in March 2025 confirms that finding, documenting a series of failures that state officials described as preventable. Among them: The county loaded final voter rolls onto its electronic pollbooks — devices used to check voters’ registration status, confirm they haven’t already voted, and issue the correct ballot to them — before Election Day, but failed to test them before shipping them across the county. It also lacked adequate plans and resources to respond when equipment malfunctioned.
 With pollbooks failing, workers couldn’t print ballots on demand or reliably verify voters’ registrations. As the machines broke down, AZCIR and Votebeat found, so did communication. Records show poll workers didn’t know when a technician would be out to fix things or exactly what had gone wrong. Preprinted emergency ballots kept in reserve in case of technical glitches began to dwindle before noon. At some locations, accessible voting machines, essential for tribal elders who only speak Navajo , also malfunctioned. And voters couldn’t just go to other polling places — the county assigned them to specific sites.
 Throughout the day, emails show that a small group of staffers worked desperately to try to fix the issues across the county, the sixth-largest in the country by area. Technicians drove hours on treacherous roads, crossing mountains and desolate mesas to deliver pollbook fixes to small communities. Still, records show the county’s Navajo precincts — those farthest from Apache’s white-majority county seat — were among the last to be fixed.
 Until they were, voting was impossible or near impossible at many sites. Low temperatures, work, and family obligations began to pull Navajo voters away from the polls — and, in some cases, records and interviews show people were turned away by overwhelmed poll workers. The secretary of state’s office also received reports of voters being improperly turned away during a court-ordered extension of polling hours, according to Fontes’ letter.
 The problems continued after Election Day. The county was so busy dealing with the fallout from in-person voting that it fell behind on verifying signatures on mail ballots. As a result, around 30 voters with signature deficiencies weren’t given the chance to fix the issue until just two days before the deadline to do so. Many of those ballots were never counted.
 Katherine Belzowski, an assistant attorney general for the Navajo Nation Department of Justice, watched the election play out from afar. She said she was initially heartbroken and horrified. Later, she said, those emotions gave way to frustration as a lawyer for the county claimed in court that the average voter was still able to cast their ballot.
 Katherine Belzowski, an assistant attorney general for the Navajo Nation Department of Justice, is pictured in Window Rock, Ariz., on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026. In 2024, Belzowski was triaging election problems from her sister’s house on the East Coast on Election Day. (Ash Ponders for Votebeat)
 That attorney said her comments were made in “good faith.” But when Votebeat and AZCIR repeated her assertion to voters and representatives of the Navajo Nation, the reactions ranged from eye rolls to full-bodied laughter. The underlying sentiment was largely the same: The “average voter” referenced in court did not include the Navajo people.
 “People were denied the right to vote left and right,” Belzowski said. “And then they were told it’s not a big deal.”
 Since 2024, Apache County has instituted some changes to its election operations, including adopting a more flexible vote center model and replacing outdated voting equipment. Shortly after early voting began this year, Belzowski said she believed the county may have “turned a corner.” Fontes said the primary election had run smoothly in Apache County and described its progress as a “story of success.”
 But Votebeat and AZCIR’s findings raise larger questions about what it will take to solve the region’s long history of disenfranchisement, and how long it has taken to address problems. In a 2018 federal lawsuit, the Navajo Nation claimed state- and county-level election practices had long disenfranchised its voters. That suit was settled the following year. And a report released earlier this year by the Native American Rights Fund found that voters in Indian Country face barriers during nearly every stage of the electoral process, particularly in Apache County and neighboring Navajo County.
 Asked whether Apache’s recent changes would be enough to address the broader problems facing Navajo voters there, Fontes offered no guarantee.
 “The answer is, [it’s] better in 2026 than it was in 2024,” Fontes said. “But it’s a fool’s errand to say that you’re going to be able to solve all the problems.”
 Amos Johnson, a member of the Navajo Nation, uses an accessible voting device to listen to instructions in Navajo at the Navajo Voters Coalition Conference at Twin Arrows near Flagstaff, Arizona, on June 18, 2026. Similar devices were glitching at some voting sites in Apache County in 2024, which may have left voters with no way to cast ballots until technicians fixed the county’s malfunctioning pollbooks. (Christopher Lomahquahu for Votebeat)
 6 a.m.: County offered little communication as machines went down
 Frances Sjoberg was among the first to realize that something was wrong.
 A lawyer with the Navajo Nation Department of Justice, Sjoberg had been assigned to observe the polls in Rock Point, a small village located about 20 miles south of the Arizona-Utah border. Within minutes of the community’s senior center opening its doors to voters, word began to spread that the printers inside weren’t working. A line began to grow.
 Sjoberg promptly called the problem in to her colleagues and Arizona State University’s Indian Legal Clinic, which often represents tribes in voting cases. Her call was the first of several from observers and voters to the clinic, based hundreds of miles away in Phoenix. 
 Torey Dolan, who’d helped with the clinic’s voter hotline since 2018, wasn’t surprised to hear that something was going wrong in Apache County, given its history of election issues. She and other attorneys had even begun sending observers to the polls with blank affidavits, prepared to document any irregularities.
 Before considering litigation, though, Dolan wanted to contact Vaughan to determine exactly what was happening and what she and observers on the ground should tell voters.
 That proved difficult. Dolan called Vaughan at 6:33 a.m., according to court documents. She hit Vaughan’s voicemail, which was full and not accepting messages, according to a court affidavit. She then called the Arizona Secretary of State’s Office and notified Belzowski, who also began making inquiries.
 Meanwhile, records show Vaughan was beginning to grasp the scale of the problem with the county’s pollbooks.
 She didn’t immediately share what she’d learned with Dolan or the Navajo Nation Department of Justice. But she did tell her team — a skeleton crew of herself, her executive assistant, and five IT techs.
 “IT IS A POLL BOOK ISSUE,” she emailed at 7:27 a.m.
 To fix it, the techs would have to travel across the county’s 11,198-square-mile expanse, an area roughly the size of Maryland. They’d need to stop at each of its 40-plus voting sites, manually updating each pollbook by plugging in a USB drive preloaded with corrected software.
 The first report of techs leaving to deploy the corrected software came at 9:09 a.m., when one went to a voting site in Concho, a non-Navajo community located about 20 minutes west of St. Johns, the county seat. 
 But a new problem was emerging. Vaughan’s techs were becoming increasingly concerned that polling locations would run out of emergency ballots before the techs arrived to fix their pollbooks. Already, some sites were reporting that they were running low. Without emergency ballots, voters at those polling places would have to rely on the county’s outdated and glitchy ExpressVote machines, accessible voting devices required by federal law to assist voters with disabilities.
 None of that, however, was in an update sent to Belzowski by the county’s attorney, Emily Craiger, at 10:12 a.m. — the first email from the county to tribal officials that day, according to records reviewed by Votebeat and AZCIR.
 Craiger said people could keep voting because emergency ballots were available. They also could use the ExpressVote machines, she said.
 Vaughan, who resigned as elections director in the weeks after the 2024 election and has since moved into a new role as the county’s human resources manager, did not respond to multiple requests for comment sent both through the county and to her directly.
 Craiger said her comments on Election Day were based on information she received from the elections department.
 10 a.m.: Voters walked away amid election chaos
 As county officials scrambled to fix the problem, voters started to leave.
 There was little that Carl R. Slater could do about it. As an elected delegate on the Navajo Nation Council, he was acting as a poll observer in Lukachukai, a small farming community nestled in mountain foothills almost three hours north of St. Johns. Slater was also informally monitoring other chapters in his council district. What he saw was a cascade of failures.
 People gather for a chapter meeting in Lukachukai, Ariz., on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026. Multiple people told reporters that they recalled what happened in 2024, when technical issues caused hourslong lines and resulted in some voters being turned away. (Ash Ponders for Votebeat)
 With pollbooks down, voters were relying on emergency ballots and ExpressVote machines. But in Round Rock, the ExpressVote machine froze in the morning, leaving emergency ballots as voters’ last resort. In St. Michaels, the polling site ran out of emergency ballots around 10 a.m., leaving voters at the mercy of the unreliable ExpressVote machine. Fort Defiance ran out of emergency ballots soon after.
 When would-be voters saw the line at Lukachukai wasn’t moving, they grew restless. Eventually, people started to leave.
 “At this point, we’ve probably turned away more people than decided the last elections,” Slater texted the Navajo Nation’s attorneys around 10:30 a.m.
 In Rock Point, Sjoberg begged people to stay in the long line that now stretched into the plaza between the chapter house and the local senior center.
 The day had begun deceptively sunny, but temperatures soon dropped and the wind sharpened. A blizzard was on the horizon, and people began to leave. Sjoberg went into triage mode.
 “I started kind of hustling,” she said. “I was primarily focused at that moment to say, ‘Will you come back to vote?’” 
 Some voters did. Crystalyne Curley, the speaker of the Navajo Nation Council, was initially told she could not vote at the precinct closest to Window Rock, the reservation’s seat of government. Instead, poll workers told her she’d have to go to Cottonwood, the precinct closest to her home community of Fish Point, an hour and 15 minutes away. It’s unclear why they did so; voters were supposed to be allowed to cast ballots outside their assigned precincts using ExpressVote machines.
 Curley made the drive, but when she got to Cottonwood, she was again told they didn’t have her ballot. Workers there directed her to return to Window Rock.
 Back where she started, minus a few gallons of gas, Curley insisted on voting and presented her ID. She was given a provisional ballot — a type of ballot that is used when there’s a question about the voter’s eligibility.
 Curley wrote down the ballot’s tracking number. Two weeks later, she followed up with county officials to check if her ballot had counted.
 “It didn’t,” Curley said. “They had no tracking of what happened.”
 Crystalyne Curley, speaker of the Navajo Nation Council, speaks with an attendee at the Navajo Voters Coalition Conference on June 18, 2026, at Twin Arrows near Flagstaff, Arizona. Curley said she was directed to polling sites in Window Rock and Cottonwood before being issued a provisional ballot on Election Day in 2024. She does not believe it was ever counted. (Christopher Lomahquahu for Votebeat)
 Others, like Wava White, couldn’t wait.
 White, now 69, arrived at Fort Defiance mid-afternoon. Voting held a special significance to White, whose uncle died in the Vietnam War. As she viewed it, her family had bled for the right to vote, so she was initially undeterred by the line ahead.
 But hours began to go by, and the line wasn’t moving. The sky grew dark. Even if White could make it to the voting booth, she still had an hour-long drive to her mother’s house.
 When she asked a poll worker how much longer it would take before she could vote, she was given an estimate of another three hours.
 Dejected, she walked away.
 Lukachukai, Rock Point, and Fort Defiance were three of the nine precincts a judge would ultimately order to remain open until 9 p.m. that evening. All of those voting locations were on the Navajo Nation, in the northern part of the county, where records suggest equipment fixes were delivered later than in the predominantly white precincts to the south.
 White wouldn’t learn until the next day that returning later to vote had been an option. Speaking with reporters inside a small coffee shop in Window Rock nearly two years later, she said she is still gutted by the experience.
 “Every four years, we vote,” White said, referring to the presidential election cycle. “And they can’t get this right.”
 7 p.m.: Court extends voting hours, but it’s too late for some voters
 An hour before the polls closed, a handful of officials and attorneys joined a virtual court hearing on the day’s voting problems.
 Earlier in the day, the Navajo Nation had notified Apache County that its lawyers planned to sue to extend voting hours due to the chaos. Craiger had called that “unnecessary,” and in an email sent just before noon, suggested that the county would have any outstanding voting sites fixed by the early afternoon.
 Hours later, though, some sites still were experiencing problems. Around 5 p.m., the Navajo Nation filed its lawsuit asking Apache County Superior Court Judge Michael Latham to extend voting by two hours across the reservation. But Vaughan and Craiger pushed back.
 “An average voter who wanted to vote today would have the opportunity to do it,” Craiger said to the court. She was based in the Phoenix area, along with most of the other lawyers on the call, and admitted that she was unfamiliar with the geography of Apache County. Still, she maintained that voters could use ExpressVote machines while technicians fixed the pollbooks and that they’d already had several hours to vote after those problems were resolved. “We acknowledge that there were longer lines than usual in Apache County, but that all voters had the ability to vote today and continue to have that ability right now,” she said.
 Yet as Craiger spoke, records show pollbooks were still malfunctioning at Canyon de Chelly, a precinct in the heart of the Navajo Nation. Emails indicate county techs had visited the site, a county office, in the morning but returned shortly after 6 p.m. to fix two pollbooks. It’s unclear whether the return visit was prompted by the same pollbook issues as that morning; records suggest no other precincts experienced further pollbook problems.
 One technician, Matt Lovell, noted in emails to Vaughan that the location had a “huge line” that evening and that he’d observed poll workers attempt to turn away voters not found in the system. Lovell, who now heads the county’s IT department, declined an interview with Votebeat and AZCIR.
 Craiger also said in court that emergency paper ballots remained available while IT staff crisscrossed the county to fix pollbooks and that “additional paper ballots were deployed to the voting locations so that voting could continue.” Vaughan would not speak with Votebeat or AZCIR to clarify the chain of events; Craiger said she was relaying information from the elections department and declined to comment further.
 Craiger further argued that spotty cell service would make it nearly impossible to quickly notify Navajo Nation polling sites about extended hours, while the reservation’s vast distances would complicate delivery of additional provisional ballots, which must be used any time polling hours are extended.
 Latham ultimately ordered a two-hour extension at only the nine sites where the day’s technical issues were most clearly documented.
 In a recent interview, Sjoberg acknowledged that the extension of hours was an imperfect solution. She described it as the best they could do under the circumstances.
 “I do not think that it redresses the issues,” she said. “I do not know that voters who left when they left came back to vote.”
 The hearing ended about 10 minutes before polls were originally scheduled to close.
 Minutes later, Canyon de Chelly’s pollbooks were finally fixed. But unlike neighboring Chinle, the site was not granted an additional two hours of voting.
 After Election Day, Apache County struggled to keep up with ballots
 Even in a normal election, a disproportionate number of voters cast provisional ballots in Apache County. There are often more questions about voters’ eligibility on tribal lands, where voters frequently lack residential addresses and might describe where they live using physical or natural landmarks, making their exact locations difficult to verify.
 But due to the chaos, the 2024 election saw even more provisional ballots cast than usual — more than 3,500. That type of ballot requires the county recorder’s office to later verify voters’ eligibility and precinct. With only a handful of full-time employees, the office quickly became overwhelmed in the days following the election.
 Keely Varvel, chief of staff at the Arizona Secretary of State’s Office, sent a handful of staffers to assist Apache County. But processing the mound of provisional ballots delayed yet another critical task, she said: verifying signatures on mail ballots.
 A home is pictured after heavy rain near Chinle, Ariz., on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026. Chinle’s voting site was among those ordered to extend voting hours after the Navajo Nation filed suit on Nov. 5, 2024, over widespread technical glitches that resulted in hourslong lines and some voters being turned away. (Ash Ponders for Votebeat) 
 In Arizona, voters can drop mail ballots off at the polls on Election Day. But state law gives only a five-day window for those ballots to be verified and for voters to fix, or “cure,” any issues with their signatures and ensure their votes are counted. That means election officials are typically under immense pressure to process mail ballots quickly and do as much voter outreach as possible before the cure deadline.
 In Apache County, records show about 30 voters were first contacted on Nov. 8, just two days before the cure deadline. Court testimony suggests that some others may not have been contacted until Nov. 9. Records show 14 voters contacted late subsequently saw their ballot rejected.
 Some likely didn’t know that the county was trying to reach them at all, as records indicate the recorder’s office lacked up-to-date contact information for many voters. When officials hit dead phone numbers, they had no way to leave a voicemail or send a text message, and no time to mail a letter.
 The recorder’s office declined to speak with Votebeat and AZCIR for this story, citing staffing limitations.
 The curing scramble led the Navajo Nation to file yet another lawsuit, this time requesting that the county extend its cure period by three days. Patty Ferguson-Bohnee, an attorney representing the Nation, said in court that tribal members had been “denied their fundamental right to vote on equal footing with Arizona citizens.”
 Craiger countered in court that the county had made “reasonable efforts” to reach voters. She called the lawsuit “speculative,” noting that lawyers hadn’t identified any voters who claimed to be disenfranchised — though Ferguson-Bohnee noted many voters “probably do not know if they are on that cure list.”
 In the end, Latham ruled for the county, finding that voters were “properly notified, pursuant to statutory requirements” of inconsistent signatures.
 But he went on to detail infrastructure challenges that might interfere with Navajo Nation voters’ ability to cast a ballot — including dirt roads, poor internet connectivity, and limited mail service.
 Latham acknowledged that additional protections could help rural and tribal voters, but he laid that responsibility squarely at the feet of state lawmakers.
 “The court lacks authority to craft legal remedies beyond what the law allows even though certain remedies may assist rural communities,” he wrote. “That is something the Arizona State Legislature has the power to address.”
 But it hasn’t.
 Years later, are changes enough to prevent another 2024?
 Much has changed in Apache County since Nov. 5, 2024.
 Earlier this year, the board of supervisors voted to start using vote centers instead of precinct-based polling places, a change long pushed by tribal and state officials that will allow voters to cast ballots at any polling site in the county. The secretary of state’s office had provided equipment that could have supported such a model in 2024 — and likely mitigated at least some of the problems voters faced there — but the county declined to use it, according to Fontes’ March 2025 letter.
 The county’s elections department, using federal grant funds, replaced its outdated ExpressVote devices. It also hired a new elections director, Megan Hill, who declined to discuss the changes made by the department. An individual familiar with the changes said the county also adopted an informal policy restricting pollbook programming updates shortly before elections, except for security purposes.
 Connette Blair poses for a portrait at the chapter house in Lukachukai, Ariz., on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026. Blair, the chapter’s vice president, said her mother had been distraught after being turned away from the polls in 2024. “She kept saying, ‘I have a right to vote. I have a right to vote,’” Blair said. (Ash Ponders for Votebeat) 
 In the recorder’s office, officials have worked to update voter records in an effort to cut down on provisional ballots and rejected mail ballots. The office also gained a new temporary employee through a state fellowship program.
 Questions about the state’s response persist. In an initial interview with Votebeat and AZCIR, Fontes recalled only that Apache’s problems appeared to involve a faulty pollbook software update. His office later provided the March 2025 letter documenting a much broader set of failures.
 In a subsequent interview, Fontes attributed his limited recollection to the volume of issues his office had dealt with since the election, noting that “so much has happened since then.” He said the letter showed that his office had thoroughly followed up with the county.
 Still, during the initial interview, Fontes acknowledged that he hadn’t pressed for every detail of the pollbook problems.
 When asked whether he should have, he paused.
 “Maybe.”
 Fontes emphasized how far the county has come, saying it has progressed “miles and miles and miles” from where it was in 2024. He also said it was worth considering whether his office should require counties to test pollbooks and limit programming changes before elections, with carveouts for critical security updates.
 Yet for all the changes Apache County has made, its longstanding staffing and funding challenges remain. In his letter, Fontes warned that the state could not continue sending employees to help Apache County process provisional ballots after elections. He urged county officials to provide adequate personnel and resources, noting the difficulty of administering elections across a vast county with a limited tax base.
 Deseree Yazzie pets her dogs in Lukachukai, Ariz., on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026. Yazzie recently turned 18 and said she is excited to vote in her first election on Nov. 3, 2026. (Ash Ponders for Votebeat) 
 Arizona law prohibits counties from accepting private funding, including grants, for election administration, even as state lawmakers have increased the responsibilities of local election officials. The law, passed in 2021 by the Republican-controlled legislature, was described as a voter confidence and election integrity measure. Sjoberg, with the Navajo Nation Department of Justice, said repealing or amending it could help counties pay for more accessible voting machines and poll workers.
 The legislature has also imposed new proof-of-residency requirements , shortened the period for curing mail ballots , and expanded automatic recounts in recent years, among other changes. Starting in 2027, county recorders will be required to remove voters from the state’s early voting list if they fail to cast a mail ballot in federal, state, or certain municipal elections over a four-year period.
 “There are so many hoops that the election directors have to jump through, and the county recorders have to jump through, that it just makes it unrealistic for any county that doesn’t have a certain amount of income,” said Belzowski, the Navajo Nation’s assistant attorney general.
 Fontes was more pointed in his criticism.
 “The legislature does not want to fund elections administration,” said Fontes, a Democrat. “They want to complain about it a lot, but they don’t want to fund it, and that’s the core of all of the issues we’ve had over many, many, many years.”
 State lawmakers could also address some of the barriers Navajo voters face at the polls. Arizona could adopt protections similar to those in neighboring New Mexico, for instance, where Native American communities have a say in polling locations, ballot box placements, and precinct boundaries. Belzowski said the voting landscape there is far easier for underresourced counties and tribal voters to navigate.
 “I think New Mexico wants to encourage people to vote,” Belzowski said. “I think Arizona is more interested in keeping people from voting.”
 Republican and Democratic leaders in the Arizona Legislature did not respond to a request for comment on whether they’d support changes to state law that could improve voting in Apache County, particularly on tribal land.
 Dolan, who now researches voting access in Indian Country at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, said she no longer directs all of her frustration toward Apache County. She described the 2024 election as a failure on the part of the state as a whole and said it will take more than changes at the county level to solve the continuous disenfranchisement of Navajo voters.
 “I realize that these are people who are working under impossible circumstances, and my frustration is dispersed amongst the institutions that made this this way,” Dolan said.
 Window Rock, Ariz., sits below cloudy skies on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026. The town is the seat of government for the Navajo Nation. Officials there have been working with Apache County to push for better elections for the reservation’s voters. (Ash Ponders for Votebeat) 
 For Navajo voters, election problems are so common they’ve become “part of the living memory there,” she added. “So, no one’s ever indignant,” she said. “They’re frustrated, but they’re not shocked.”
 That history led White, of Fort Defiance, to make a different plan for voting this year. This time, she arranged to receive her ballot by mail and said she would drop it off at a county office.
 She told Votebeat and AZCIR she would be watching what happens on Election Day.
 “If there’s a glitch, fix it,” she said, adding that she was “sure something would have been done really quick” if pollbooks failed en masse in Phoenix.

 Radical Reconstruction: Looking to the Past To Move Forward
 Seamus Love 
 Oct 27, 2026 
 The last 11 years of electoral politics have plunged our nation into new lows: withdrawal and reentry into Middle Eastern conflicts, a politicized public health response during a pandemic, an attempted coup of the American government, and continual police brutality against people of color. Donald Trump’s existence on the political stage, in office or out, has held our nation hostage through repeated crises, leading us to the most divided time in our nation since the Civil War. The path forward for our young country doesn’t just require new ideas: we need to finally follow through on Reconstruction.
 A blip in American history, Abraham Lincoln’s post-Civil War vision , called Reconstruction, was the proposed path forward for Southern reentry into American life. In exchange for loyalty to the Union and some guarantees of black civil protection, Lincoln prepared to readmit secessionist states into the Union, albeit with political restraints on numerous Confederate leaders. 
 Reconstruction was a bold stance by Lincoln, whose assassination prevented him from witnessing the civil rights gains made during the stage in American history he worked tirelessly to usher in. Under successive presidents Andrew Johnson and Ulysses S. Grant, the Reconstruction Era actualized much of Lincoln’s vision. In twelve years, “Radical Reconstruction” led to the ratification of the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments, saw former enslaved men and Union heroes such as Robert Smalls elected to state and federal office across the South, and culminated in the passage of the Civil Rights Act of 1875.
 But its staying power was marred by racial tension, loosened restrictions on political participation for former Confederate leaders, and political strife inside both parties over Reconstruction’s impact on White Southerners. The election of Rutherford B. Hayes in the 1876 presidential election ended Reconstruction and paved the way for Jim Crow across the American South, undoing the initial steps needed for a young country to learn from its past. 
 It took almost 90 more years for America to progress closer to Reconstruction’s intent with the Civil Rights and Voting Rights legislation of the 1960’s, and it’s still evident today that our baby steps toward addressing equal rights weren’t enough. 
 From the President’s petition to the Supreme Court to dismiss mail-in ballots to the gutting of the Voting Rights Act via the Louisiana v. Callais decision , 2026 alone has proven the need to aggressively expand voting rights for African Americans. America’s post-Trump era is merely 28 months away, and our nation can’t expect to brush off generations of wounds and move forward: we need to reflect on what we failed to accomplish post-Civil War and get back to the “Radical Reconstruction” our country still desperately needs.
 It seems impossible to speculate on how to close the chapter on a period that officially ended 149 years ago, but the starting point is obvious: The John R. Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act . A piece of legislation that would revitalize the Voting Rights Act of 1965 , this bill would protect communities of color against racial gerrymandering and revamp protections for polling places and workers against any form of threat or violence.
 The United States is at more than a crossroads; its soul is under attack. If we truly want to recover the soul of America, irrespective of party lines, then turning the clock on Reconstruction and delivering new voting rights legislation is the honest way forward.
 Like President Rutherford B. Hayes, Donald Trump is just the current impediment to our path forward as a country. After President Trump leaves the White House in January 2029, Reconstruction could finally get us back on track and ensure that everyone, regardless of race, religion, or political affiliation, has an America whose laws treat them equally – fulfilling the original intent of Abraham Lincoln’s “Radical Reconstruction."
 Seamus Love is a speechwriter and Democratic strategist.

 Frustrated with the two-party system? An argument for a tripartisan alternative: an Independent Caucus of 5-6 senators with leverage over major legislation.
 donald_gruener/Getty Images
 The Two-Party System or What?
 Dave Anderson 
 Oct 27, 2026 
 The evidence continues to come in -- lately from USA Facts and the Unpopulist -- that the majority of American voters don't like our two-party political system. Yet there is no consensus on what we want to replace it with. 
 There does seem to be an assumption that if you don't like the two-party system , then you want a political system which supports more than two parties, namely a multi-party system.
 New America's Lee Drutman , the author of Breaking the Two-Party Doom Loop , has made the best case yet for a multi-party system. For those who want a multi-party political system, read his very engaging, well-argued book. 
 Still, the assumption that the alternative to the two-party system, at least the democratic alternative, is the multi-party system needs to be challenged.
 It may be true that most Americans would prefer a multi-party system to our two-party system. So, turn us into a multi-party democracy like Europe, Japan, South Korea, Canada, and Australia, but leave out the parliamentary structure. Thus, a presidential/legislative structure, but multi-party rather than two-party.
 The problem with this way of framing the situation is that many Americans probably do not understand that there is an alternative to a two-party system that is not about having more political parties (and having them in a system that welcomes them), even with ranked-choice voting, impartial redistricting committees, fusion voting, and proportional representation. 
 No, there is an alternative to the two-party system, which has nothing to do with political parties.
 So how can this be?
 Well, very simply. There is an alternative I have been defending for three years, namely a system that seeks tripartisanship and not bipartisanship, one which does so by developing an Independent Caucus of 5-6 U.S. Senators. An Independent Caucus can be developed in the House also, but an IC is less needed in the House.
 In the Senate, an IC could have enormous leverage, where votes could be needed not only to reach 51 votes but to reach 60 votes on major policy bills. 
 The IC, as I conceive it, would be made up of senators from diverse political perspectives. They would not all be centrists.
 They can be elected as independents, convert from a major party to independent, or remain independent if they are elected as independents (like Sanders and King) rather than caucus with either major party. 
 The IC is not a political party. It would be much smaller; it would have no central organizing committee, and it would not be a fundraising machine for a platform. No, the IC would be a group of senators who are driven by their own values, beliefs, and interests. But they would realize that they will only have power if, at times, some or most or all of them vote together to support a bill up for consideration.
 Why the IC could hang together is a very complicated question. It is just as complicated as the question multi-party system advocates must answer about how they expect to get laws passed state by state or nationally that would create the election reforms that their system would need to support many political parties.
 Suffice to say that no one in politics or life gets everything they want. But hanging together would enable the IC to get some of their favorite bills passed, and those times when they had to hold their nose would be for the good of the country.
 The two-party system can be fundamentally changed without creating a multi-party system and without election reform measures that pose monumental obstacles as a matter of state or federal politics.
 There is, thus, a false dichotomy in many political circles between a two-party system vs. a multi-party system. It is assumed that there are two alternatives to structuring American politics, one which has two parties that have power and one which has three, four, five, or more parties that have power.
 There is a middle position, a way to empower over 60 million Americans who do not identify with either major party. The middle position promotes tripartisanship, not bipartisanship or systems that empower four parties or five parties or more.
 We can fix the two-party system without trying to empower other political parties. We can fix the system by empowering a group of 5-6 U.S. Senators from diverse perspectives.
 Dave Anderson edited " Leveraging: A Political, Economic and Societal Framework ," has taught at five universities and ran for the Democratic nomination for a Maryland congressional seat in 2016.

 (==Gabriel Cárdenas for Votebeat
 Election Officials Are Scrambling To Process Voter Registration Backlog Using a System They Say Does Not Work
 Natalia Contreras, Votebeat Texas 
 Oct 19, 2026 
 At 6 p.m. a few days after the state sent Randall County election administrator Shannon Lackey a backlog of 3,388 of voter registration records, she was still at her desk, processing them after a full day of work.
 She planned to stay late and get as much done as she could, then keep working from home. Lackey, whose department has five employees, isn’t expecting overtime pay or compensatory time off to make up for the extra work caused by the state error .
 The most frustrating part, she said, was that the state’s voter registration and management system, known as TEAM, was making it harder to get through the backlog.
 “I just got a message saying ‘an error occurred’,” Lackey said while on the phone with a Votebeat reporter. “I cannot tell you how many times I get that message, ‘an error occurred,’ so I’m just clicking. Nothing’s happening. I can’t work right now.”
 She said her only choice is to push through.
 “I have to get this done” she said, but “how are we going to fix it? And if it’s not fixable, where do we go from here? Because this is unacceptable.”
 Local election officials across the state have raised concerns about TEAM since the state rolled out a long-awaited upgrade more than a year ago. Now they must use the system to resolve a backlog of hundreds of thousands of voter registration records and updates state officials sent them due to a software error with the Texas Department of Public Safety web portal. Many say the issues with TEAM are making the backlog harder to resolve at a critical time.
 State officials discovered the error just weeks before today’s deadline for Texans to register to vote in time for the critical midterm elections. Election officials are already contending with the typical high volume of voter registration applications delivered in person and by mail at the last minute in the coming days.
 Some better-resourced and larger county election departments have been able to quickly resolve their backlogs with help from outside vendors, but they’re also still reporting problems interacting with TEAM.
 Election officials said it is still difficult to verify voters’ eligibility when processing voter registration applications, and process mail-in ballots in TEAM, among other tasks.
 “Based on the direct experiences of county election officials across the state, it has become evident that these problems are the result of fundamental system architecture failures by the state’s voter registration database vendor, Civix,” the Texas Association of County Election Officials said in a statement last week.
 With the election just weeks away, the state should “ensure the delivery and maintenance of reliable voter registration database software” before any further payments are made to Civix, which is based in Louisiana, the statement said.
 Civix did not respond to a request for comment.
 The Texas Secretary of State’s Office said it’s offering counties grants to reimburse their costs to process the backlogged applications.
 In an emailed statement, Alicia Pierce, the spokesperson for the secretary of state’s office, said the agency has communicated directly with counties about TEAM “on a continual basis.” Pierce said the agency conducted trainings throughout the state for the rollout and continues to offer webinars. “We send weekly emails with updates on production builds and development work, and we host monthly calls for counties to ask questions,” she wrote.
 “Texas has had seven successful elections since the rollout of the newly developed TEAM,” she added. “Additional features addressing county concerns will be rolled out soon as we all prepare for the November election.”
 The agency has resolved some functionality issues with TEAM and has improved it some since its July 2025 launch, election officials told Votebeat, but fixes often take months. In other cases, when one problem is resolved, another pops up.
 Some voting rights advocates say local election officials have enough burdens without adding technological problems to the mix.
 “If I had to log on to a system every day and have no idea if it was going to work today like it worked yesterday, I think I would lose my mind,” said Emily Eby French, policy director at Common Cause Texas. “But we are asking county officials to follow hundreds and hundreds of statutes in the Texas Election Code, keep ballots safe, protect the security of the elections, while not knowing how or if TEAM will work for them.” 
 Election officials say promises still unmet
 In January 2024, at an annual gathering of election officials, the state showed an early video demonstration of new features the upgraded TEAM system would have. They said it would help election officials complete tasks more quickly and efficiently.
 Hundreds of election officials clapped and cheered in excitement. They’d been waiting years for such upgrades. 
 But “those promises are still unmet,” Kristin Miles, the Bastrop County elections administrator and current president of the Texas Association of County Election Officials, said in an interview. “We’re not even at basic functionality, much less bells and whistles that had county election officials excited back then.”
 Texas promised to pay Civix $17 million, and up to $36 million if the state renews the contract in October 2027, public records show. The secretary of state’s office said the cost is covered by a mix of state dollars and federal funds earmarked for improving election administration.
 Officials in each of the state’s 254 counties interact with the TEAM system on a daily basis to conduct voter list maintenance and manage elections. Roughly 18 counties use state-approved outside vendors to manage their voter registration lists, but must still sync their data with TEAM daily and rely on TEAM for other essential functions.
 Three local election officials told Votebeat they are struggling with verifying voters’ eligibility, a key step that must be done in TEAM.
 That step confirms a voter’s name, date of birth, and partial Social Security number or driver’s license number matches state records, essentially ensuring that the registrant is who they say they are. It’s an automated process, and the majority of the time it works. But in some cases, election officials said they have waited weeks — up to 60 days — for that verification, and they aren’t sure why.
 A long delay risks that the voter doesn’t show up on the rolls when they try to actually vote, said Michelle Allcon, the Smith County elections administrator.
 “I can’t tell what that application is missing so we can fix it. It’s just stuck,” Allcon said. She said election administrators first flagged the problem in May. “Then those voters are calling me, asking ‘what’s going on? Why haven’t I gotten my voter registration certificate?’ And we look into it and see that there’s no action.”
 Allcon, along with other election officials, said the secretary of state’s office typically confirms creation of an IT ticket to resolve the problem, but isn’t necessarily able to give a timeline for the fix.
 Some election officials say they have come up with workarounds. Trudy Hancock, the Brazos County election administrator, said her staff has created a spreadsheet to track which mail ballots have been sent and received, as well as to sort them by voter ID number, name, and date, a feature that TEAM doesn’t have. In TEAM, her staff isn’t able to select a batch of mail-in ballot records at once to mark them as sent or received. Instead, they have to be updated one by one, which is time-consuming. The spreadsheet helps the elections team organize the ballots before marking them in the TEAM system. Her staff is keeping track of more than 1,800 mail ballots, Hancock said last week.
 Although no technology rollout is ever perfect, other states have taken early steps to try and avoid problems later.
 A 2024 report on four states that launched voter registration systems — Arizona, Nevada, Georgia, and Rhode Island — emphasized involving local election officials, who it described as the main users of such systems, from the start.
 But in Texas, local election officials say they had little input. Miles, Lackey, Hancock and others say their testing of the system occurred only a couple of months before the TEAM upgrade went live.
 Election officials say they’ll figure it out, but worry the public is losing trust
 The counties that use outside vendors rely less heavily on TEAM, though they still must use it. But those vendors can be costly, while TEAM is free.
 Dallas County’s election department uses an outside vendor. That’s how they were able to quickly get through a backlog of nearly 70,000 records sent to them after the DPS error, Elections Administrator Paul Adams said in an interview.
 “There are other counties where either they don’t have that access to vendors or they have limited staff. So for some counties it’s going to be difficult, but everybody has contingency plans,” Adams said.
 He said the main concern is what news of the backlog — and the state error that caused it — is doing to voters’ confidence.
 “People are already concerned about the election; you start adding additional things onto it, and your voters are now concerned about the process,” he said.

These terms were marked by distinct economic hardships, structural imbalances, or severe financial crises.
 Destabilizing Partisan Protectionism 
 To compensate for a lack of broad popular support, some non-popular vote winners leaned heavily into aggressive, special-interest economic policies—such as hyper-protectionist tariffs—to satisfy the narrow geographic coalitions that elected them.
 Benjamin Harrison (1889–1893): Harrison lost the popular vote but won the Electoral College by carrying key industrial states. To reward his base, Harrison championed the McKinley Tariff of 1890, which raised import duties to historic highs of nearly 50%.
 The Fallout: The tariff triggered retaliatory trade measures, depleted the federal surplus via reckless spending, and severely strained the U.S. gold supply through the concurrent Sherman Silver Purchase Act. This volatile mixture directly triggered the Panic of 1893, one of the most devastating depressions in American history. The 1894 midterm elections ballot-box response delivered the largest incumbent-party reversal in U.S. history. Voters used the ballot box to punish the incumbent party, stripping them of 127 house seats, their remaining 93 seats represent a preservation of 42.27% of their peak 220-seat strength, and usuring in the Progressive Era (1890s to 1920s).
